newsitem.title: USA: US bonds end lower after strong April housing data.
newsitem.headline: US bonds end lower after strong April housing data.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices ended lower on Friday after the government reported a brisk pace of new housing starts in April.
The Commerce Department said new housing starts rose 2.6 percent last month to a 1.473 million annualized rate.
Wall Street economists had forcast, on average, that housing starts occurred at a 1.43 million annualized rate.
"The stronger-than-expected housing report sent us down hard soon after the open," said Chris Rupkey, vice president and financial economist at Bank of Tokyo/Mitsubishi.
"The market tried to struggle back, but got hit again by the Michigan consumer sentiment index," he said.

The University of Michigan's preliminary index of consumer sentiment for May rose to 104.6 from 101.4 in the final April index, sources said. The index's current conditions component fell to 113.9 from 115.2, while the expectations index rose to 98.6 from 92.5, the sources said.
The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond finished at 96-14/32, down 16/32, to yield 6.91 percent.
"Most of the damage occurred around the housing numbers," said A.G. Edwards & Sons fixed-income strategist Bill Hornbarger. "Those really pushed the market down."
Besides that, "you had a day where investors were sitting on the sidelines just watching and waiting."
What investors are waiting for is the Federal Reserve's Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting on May 20.
Analysts said the markets are uncertain as to whether policymakers will decide to push the short-term Federal funds rate up another 25 basis points or leave it at its current level of 5-1/2 percent.

Stephen Plant, I.D.E.A. Treasury market strategist, said the market was a little vulnerable on Friday because prices were already discounting a slower economy. Some investors were inclined to take profits before the FOMC meeting, he said.

"This week the market began to think that a Fed rate hike was less likely and now that prices have discounted that and we get closer to May 20, people are thinking, 'We've made a lot of money; let's take some profits,'" Plant said.
While prices did fall half a point at the long end of the maturity range, the market's performance was a long way from collapse, participants said.

"People are thoroughly confused about what's going to happen," said Rupkey. "Number one is whether the Fed says yeah or nay on rates. And number two they're not confident of their ability to guess which way the market is going to go even if the Fed changes rates because we've gone back and forth so much this week."
Rupkey said if the Fed raises interest rates, the two-year note yield would have to move up 20 basis points.
"I can't imagine it would stay here at 6.25 percent," he said. "But if there's that much risk of a rate hike, the market is not really trying to discount it much."
"The profile of the day was selling and we closed near the lows, but we didn't break Thursday's low," said Rupkey. "We didn't run away on the downside."

The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond ended at 96-30/32, up 7/32 to yield 6.87 percent. The 10-year Treasury note closed aat 99-24/32, up 3/32 to yield 6.66 percent. Five-year notes ended at 100-15/32, up 2/32 to yield 6.51 percent.
Near the shorter end of the maturity range, two-year notes closed at 100-9/32, up 1/32 to yield 6.22 percent.
Six-month and year-bill rates each slipped one basis point to 5.28 percent and 4.98 percent, respectively. Three-month bill rates dropped five basis points to 4.98 percent.
(( -- North American Treasury Desk 212-859-1679))
